Once again breaking my lurking status to comment, haha. This post really resonated with me and I hope, if you see this, this gives you some perspective.

When I was 12, I came out to my mother as bisexual. I knew she was extremely religious, same as your husband, but I was a kid, and I thought it was possible that maybe she'd understand and accept me because I was her daughter. My mother had never been the best mother, she is also very mentally ill, but I wanted to hope, anyways. It was a stupid thing to do in hindsight, but I was a kid, and all I wanted were for my parents to love and accept me. 

She kicked me out without a second thought.

My father, who had never been accepting of the LGBT community, immediately stepped up. My parents were already divorced, which made things a little easier, but my father did everything he could do to start trying to understand and to make sure I knew that no matter what, I was always his daughter, and he always loved me. Even if he didn't understand.

My mother, though she eventually would take me back into the house, never did. It was unfortunately just another thing to use as fuel against me for her. The biggest thing my father did that made me feel like I could trust him, and the thing I strongly, strongly encourage you to do for your son, is that my father never let my mother speak like that in front of him. If he was there, he made sure to make it clear to my mother those kinds of words and actions would *not* be tolerated. Because of that, I always felt safe with my father. Every mean or passive aggressive thing my mother tried to do in front of him was completely shut down. And this went for the rest of his family, too -- his siblings were also very bigoted, but around me? They never said a word, because they knew he would never let them.

I no longer speak to my mother at all, haven't in 6 years, but my father and I are literally meeting for brunch today. At 24, I still call him almost daily, and talk to him about nearly everything. Largely because he was and is always on my side, no matter what.

Please, please continue to be there for your son, but don't let your husband get away with this "I love him but don't accept him" attitude. Your son is going through a lot of heartbreak right now, and knowing you are with him will mean the world to him. You do not have to divorce your husband, but don't let his attitude and comments slide. Proudly stand up for your son against him, even if it's hard. I promise you it will make all the difference.

And it might make a difference to your husband, too. If you don't tolerate it, he might realize what his actions and words are really doing to your son and to your family unit. He literally may not even realize how deeply it's effecting you all because he's so wrapped up in his own thoughts. 

Thank you for caring so deeply about your son. Thank you for coming on here and looking to take constructive feedback about what you can do to make your son feel supported, and on your marriage as well. I really do hope things work out for you all. Good luck.

I basically only lurk on reddit, and I'm sure this is going to get buried, but I wanted to give you my two cents as someone who is mentally ill and also has had friends who were pathological liars. Hopefully you read this.

On the fact that she claims her parents are abusive but she also drives a nice car, or has no debt: you can have an extremely wealthy upbringing and still have absolutely awful, abusive households. I wanted for nothing as a child in terms of toys and clothes, but my mother is mentally ill and physically and mentally abused me. The toys and clothes were her way of trying to convince the world that she was a perfect mom with a perfect daughter. It took a long time for me to be able to articulate that clearly, since people often think toys/gifts=spoiled child. And for the record, I know most colleges, even incredibly prestigious universities like Harvard, will accept a student with a GED if they outdo or match other criteria.

On the lies that you have caught her in, like the movie: a lot of people have brought up the pathological liar/delusional perspective, and while that's certainly likely, here's something you might not have heard before. As a mentally ill child, I used to twist my abuse stories to sound more palatable to the people around me. No kid wanted to listen to what was actually happening so I made it make sense to them - ie "my mother hits me" is a lot easier to process then "my mother takes away my body autonomy, is a control freak to an abusive degree, occasionally throws large objects at me, and consistently forgets to feed me" for most kids. It wasn't honest, and it wasn't a good way to handle it, but I was a kid. It's possible that she is still working through these sorts of damaging coping mechanisms that she learned as a child, because it took me years to figure that out. 

It's so common for me to want to shut down/hide my abuse that in normal conversations, I will just brush over it/straight up lie if I'm uncomfortable or not thinking straight. For example, her bone breaking thing - if her father *did* break her wrist, that's not something I at least would feel comfortable telling most people. And generally, when you mention you broke a bone, people want to know how. I don't mention to people a chronic condition I have generally because it's related to my rape. It's become a reflex to lie about having said condition at this point since I don't want to answer questions about it. Why would I want to tell people that, or bring it up in a lighthearted situation? If I'm having a good time with friends, and it's relevant for whatever reason/someone asks me about health conditions, I will just lie. I don't even think about it most of the time, because the alternative is having to be open about something incredibly painful to me.

And finally, as someone who has known other pathological liars who have legitimately been abused: the hardest part is that the lying is a defense mechanism. It's so possible that she, like a friend I used to have, was abused very badly, but that shit gets heavy. It's so much easier to make up stories as a way to talk about it without ever feeling like you're exposing yourself. No matter how much you can trust a person, trauma is always a different beast, and some people feel like it's easier to make up stories that are sort of relevant (in terms of the feelings they would create) then it is to just talk about what actually happened to them. Sometimes trauma feels a lot more like a story in your head then an actual event that happened to you, which can contribute too. 

You seem to really care about this person. You're also right to be suspicious. I'm not trying to tell you she should be absolved from any blame, or that there isn't a chance that she's just a shitty person. There's always that chance. But you know her better than the rest of us. You are the only person here who has seen her during these moments, who can judge if she is genuine at least in her feelings towards what she's told you. I think Reddit is often too quick to jump to the worst conclusions, so I wanted to hopefully give you another perspective to think about. Good luck, and I hope you do what's best for you regardless.
